title: Knowledge Check 10: Lessons 73-82
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 73-82 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per lesson 73, why should you run the platform on cost per completed task rather than cost per token?
options: Because cost per token is a vanity metric: per-token prices keep falling while total bills keep rising, since the work-per-task multiplier grows faster than the price per unit comes down, and a per-token view hides expensive output tokens and retries
Because cost per token is always higher and easier for finance to negotiate down
Because cost per token does not exist as a metric in any provider's invoice
Because cost per completed task only includes the model output and ignores all input tokens
questions.explanation: The lesson states cost per token is a vanity metric: per-million-token prices keep falling while enterprise AI bills still rise, because agentic workflows grow the work-per-task multiplier faster than the price per unit falls. A per-token view also hides expensive output tokens and retries. The unit that actually governs money is cost per completed task, traced across every input, output, retry, and sub-agent step.

questions.question: A team cuts per-call context size by 40% but the change triggers 67% more model calls. Using the lesson's three-lever cost identity, why does this fail to save money?
options: Because the routing classifier always spends more tokens than the context it saved

Because a 40% reduction in context multiplied by a 67% increase in calls reaches roughly break-even under the linear cost model, so the save on lever one is spent back on lever two, the call count, and each added call also retransmits the growing context on every turn
Because reducing context size automatically increases output tokens by the same amount
Because prompt caching is disabled whenever the context changes, wiping out all savings
questions.explanation: The lesson cites Infosys: a 40% reduction in per-call context that triggers 67% more calls reaches break-even under the linear cost model, because 0.60 multiplied by 1.67 is approximately 1.00. The interaction compounds because each added call retransmits accumulated history rather than a fixed-size payload. This is the substitution effect the lesson warns about: naive optimizations shift cost between levers rather than removing it.

questions.question: A team wants to move a workload from a managed LLM API to self-hosted GPU infrastructure. Per lesson 73, what is the correct economic decision rule?
options: Self-host whenever the workload is narrow, because narrow tasks always justify fixed hardware
Never self-host, because managed APIs are always cheaper than owning GPUs
Decide on enthusiasm for open-source models rather than measured volume

Model the crossover against metering data and move the workload only when sustained GPU utilization clears roughly 60% to 70%, because below about 30% utilization self-hosting is usually more expensive than the API and the economics only tilt sharply in favor of self-hosting at high utilization
questions.explanation: The lesson applies a utilization threshold: on dedicated GPU inference, below roughly 30% realized utilization self-hosting is frequently more expensive than the API alternative, and above 60% to 70% utilization the economics tilt sharply toward self-hosting. The strategic move is to use telemetry to identify the highest-volume, narrowest tasks and move only those, and to start self-hosting only after metering confirms enough volume and utilization to justify the fixed infrastructure spend.

questions.question: Per lesson 74, why does a security review for an agent have to start with assets and never-boundaries rather than jumping straight to the attack list?
options: Because the attack list is the same for every agent and needs no local context

Because you cannot decide what to protect against a threat until you have said what that threat is meant to reach, and the asset list in an AI system extends beyond databases to include the integrity of the context the model reasons over and the integrity of the agent's actions
Because threat modeling only cares about confidentiality of stored data
Because naming assets is optional and only matters for auditors after launch
questions.explanation: The lesson follows Microsoft's AI threat-modeling guidance: start by being explicit about what you are protecting. Assets extend beyond databases and credentials to user safety, trust, privacy, the integrity of prompts and contextual data, and the integrity of the agent's actions. The assets exercise also forces the honest question of what action the system should never take, which gives the threat set something concrete to attach to.

questions.question: A support agent can read a customer email, retrieve a policy document, update a CRM row, and call a refund tool. An attacker embeds hostile instructions inside a document the agent will retrieve. Using the lesson's threat model, why does the refund call get stopped even though the model's intent has moved?
options: Because the model's refusal training recognizes the embedded text and refuses to act
Because the retrieved document is validated and rejected before it enters the context window

Because the injection can move the model's intent but cannot override the deterministic boundaries around it: a hard verify step that requires a matching copied receipt, a support-tier identity with no refund permission, and a default-deny policy that logs every call
Because the prompt is hashed against a known-good registry and any new version is dropped
questions.explanation: The worked example shows the injection targets the model, and the defense lives in the wiring around it. The refund tool is gated behind deterministic verify logic that requires a verified matching receipt, the support-tier identity has no refund permission at all, and the gateway applies default-deny so the refund call only succeeds for the human escalation path. What stops the attack is not the model being careful; it is that the action is unachievable from where the agent sits.

questions.question: Per lesson 74, what is the most important requirement for the residual-risk column of a written security review?
options: Every threat must be mitigated so no residual risk remains
Each accepted risk gets a named owner who writes down why it is accepted, because a review that records who accepted each remaining risk is the record a governance board and auditor actually want
Residual risk is only recorded for threats above a token-spend threshold
The column is populated automatically by the vendor's security scanner
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that the residual-risk column is the most important and the one most teams skip. Every accepted risk needs a name and a reason, or it is not a decision, it is an omission. A review that ends with every row mitigated is not being honest, because no agent is fully hardened. Recording who accepted each remaining risk is what makes the review an auditable system that a governance board can sign.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Incident Response for Agents", what must happen before any rollback, restart, or credential revocation when you confirm an agent incident?
options: Export or snapshot the incident window's trace tree to storage independent of the production system
Delete the affected sessions' logs so the bad behavior is not preserved
Revert to the last known-good prompt immediately to stop the bleeding
Restart the agent to clear its in-memory state before investigating
questions.explanation: The lesson: a rollback swaps the running version and a restart clears in-memory state, and either can overwrite or orphan the exact span-level record the postmortem needs. So you freeze or export the trace first, to storage independent of production, before any recovery action.

questions.question: The answer agent that made the mistake sent 40 incorrect refund emails to customers. Per the lesson's rollback-by-action-class framework, why is this class hard to roll back, and what is the correct substitute?
options: Emails are idempotent and can be reversed like a database write, so no follow-up is needed
A sent message cannot be unsent, so the response is a follow-up communication template, a legal review of that follow-up, and extraction of the impacted-customer list
The emails can be recalled because the agent has read access to the customer inboxes
Restarting the agent makes the sent emails untraceable so they can be ignored
questions.explanation: The lesson groups customer communications as the class where a sent message cannot be unsent. The rollback table specifies the substitute action: a follow-up communication template under legal review plus the impacted-customer list extraction.

questions.question: In the MTTD-for-Agents detection chain, if the entire fourteen-day delay before awareness sits between Signal and Trigger, what is the root cause you should fix, per the lesson?
options: Missing instrumentation on the agent's action path
Poor alerting hygiene, because the pager did not reach the operator
A tripwire that never fired on the signal
The human took too long to acknowledge the page
questions.explanation: The lesson maps each gap in the chain to its own root cause: a delay between Action and Signal is missing instrumentation, between Signal and Trigger is a tripwire that never fired, and between Page and Acknowledgement is alerting hygiene. Here the gap is Signal to Trigger, so the missing tripwire is the fix.

questions.question: An operator wants to reconstruct what an agent did in production three weeks ago and says she can simply set temperature to zero and re-run the agent to reproduce it. Why is that wrong, per lesson 76?
options: Because temperature only controls the token sampling step, while the logits feeding it vary with batch composition and GPU numerics, so a failing run usually cannot be reproduced by running again, and reproducibility must come from the recorded log
Because temperature zero makes the model refuse to call tools, so the re-run would halt on the first tool call
Because setting temperature to zero disables trace capture, so nothing is recorded on the re-run
Because all cloud inference providers forbid temperature zero for agent workloads
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that temperature controls only the token sampling step; the logits that feed that choice come out of floating point operations that are not bit-identical run to run, influenced by which batch the request lands in and which GPU it hits. OpenAI's seed parameter improves reproducibility without guaranteeing it, and Anthropic notes temperature zero is not fully deterministic. So a failing run usually cannot be reproduced by running again, and deterministic replay instead reconstructs it from the recorded log.

questions.question: A compliance investigator must hand over the trace of a flagged agent run and prove it was not altered since the night it was written. Following lesson 76, what is the correct procedure?
options: Replay the run live against the production system and show the output matches
Recompute the message digest of the exported trace and compare it with the hash recorded at write time, stored out of band, while working from copies and keeping a logged chain of custody
State that the log is on an append-only store and ask that it be trusted
Ask the engineer who restored the agent to confirm nothing was changed
questions.explanation: The lesson applies the NIST SP 800-86 forensic practice of integrity hashing: compute the message digest at collection, store the hash somewhere it cannot be changed, work only on copies, and re-hash to confirm the values still match. A single changed bit produces a completely different digest. The chain of custody, who exported what and when, supports the integrity claim.

questions.question: A company's agent processes personal data and regulators ask it to demonstrate compliance with data-protection principles. Per lesson 76, what role does the agent audit record play?
options: It is optional decoration that carries no regulatory meaning

GDPR Article 5(2) requires the controller to be able to demonstrate compliance, and the unaltered agent trace is that documentation, built in the record-keeping shape that EU AI Act Article 12 requires for high-risk systems
It is useful only for debugging, never for regulators
It replaces the obligation to comply with the underlying rules themselves
questions.explanation: The lesson frames compliance as the ability to demonstrate. GDPR Article 5(2) makes the controller responsible for, and able to demonstrate compliance with, the processing principles, which the ICO frames as keeping evidence of what you did. The EU AI Act's Article 12 requires high-risk systems to allow automatic logging organized around traceability. The unaltered agent trace is the mechanism that makes both demonstrations real.

questions.question: Your team needs an agent to obtain a verdict from another team's autonomous agent that runs its own planning loop. Per the lesson, which boundary are you crossing and why does it matter?
options: An agent boundary, so the peer belongs behind A2A where the task id, cancellation, partial artifacts, and input requests survive; wrapping it as an MCP tool discards exactly those
A tool boundary, so MCP is correct because every remote capability should be exposed as a callable function
Either protocol works identically because both use JSON-RPC 2.0, so pick the one with fewer dependencies
An agent boundary, so the client should import the peer's prompt and tool definitions to keep behavior consistent
questions.explanation: The lesson separates the two edges: MCP standardizes reaching tools and data, while A2A exists for independent, opaque agents and preserves the durable task, cancellation, artifacts, and input requests. Wrapping an agent as a tool throws those away.

questions.question: A client submits a task and the peer returns TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED. According to the lesson, what is the correct client behavior?
options: Treat it as a failure and open a new task with a fresh messageId
Poll GetTask without limit until the state changes to completed
Treat it as an interrupted state, supply the missing information in another message bound to the same task id, and keep the context
Cancel the task and retry the whole request later with a different payload
questions.explanation: INPUT_REQUIRED and AUTH_REQUIRED are interrupted states, not terminal ones. The lesson warns that clients handling only completed and failed will strand work that was waiting on one clarification, and that resending as new work loses the task continuity.

questions.question: An agent discovers a peer through a well-known Agent Card and reads its skill description and examples into its own context. Which stance does the lesson prescribe?
options: The card is authoritative, so a declared capability is enough authorization to delegate whatever the description claims
A valid JWS signature proves the peer is trustworthy and its outputs can skip downstream validation
The card body can be ignored at runtime because versions change too often to check capabilities
The card is provider-controlled text and a claim: check capabilities and version at runtime, decide delegation from your own policy, and treat the descriptions as untrusted data
questions.explanation: The lesson calls the card an advertisement written by the party asking for work, notes that skill names, descriptions, and examples are free-form remote text entering a prompt, and states that signature verification answers origin only, not trustworthiness or accuracy.

questions.question: A team is automating a document intake process. The steps are always the same, the number of documents varies by batch, and every extraction output can be checked against a JSON schema. Per the lesson's five-question test, what shape should they build?
options: An autonomous agent, because the document count varies and the model should decide how many to read
An orchestrator-workers system with no fixed outer structure, so subtasks can be discovered per batch
A workflow, because the steps are enumerable, the step count is bounded by the batch, and a validator can decide whether each step succeeded
A workflow only if the model is removed entirely, since any model call inside durable code breaks determinism
questions.explanation: The lesson scores enumerability, bounded step count, and validator-gated success as workflow answers, and warns that a wrong branch is what pushes toward code-controlled paths. It also states the model may do real work inside a workflow, but never chooses the next step.

questions.question: In the contract renewal worked example, the agent-shaped version produced three problems: skipped documents, ungated extraction flowing into a recommendation, and a bill that varied by a factor of three. What does the lesson identify as the root cause?
options: The model was too small for the task, so extraction quality collapsed without control
The agent was doing what agents do, deciding, when the design never said which decisions were its to make; the fix is moving it to the exception queue where judgment pays
The tools were misconfigured, so the agent could not see two of the forty documents
The workflow engine's retry policy was missing, which caused the cost variance across runs
questions.explanation: The lesson frames all three as controls that were removed rather than a worse model, and prescribes moving the agent to the rung where its judgment adds value: the exception queue, where the path genuinely varies and a person checks the output.

questions.question: You want an agent to run as one step inside a durable workflow. Which seam contract does the lesson require before the first run?
options: Let the agent write directly to the workflow's event history so the engine can replay its reasoning later
Give the agent an unbounded iteration budget so it can always finish, and log the transcript for audit
Call the model directly from the deterministic workflow body so the engine can cache the result on replay
A typed input schema, a typed output schema, validation at the boundary, an idempotency key, a timeout, a cost ceiling, and a defined escalation when validation fails
questions.explanation: The lesson lists exactly those seven items as the seam contract and warns that every undefined one becomes an incident. It also warns that a model call inside deterministic workflow code returns a different answer on replay and breaks the history match.

questions.question: A team builds an LLM-based risk classifier to decide which agent actions need human approval, and feeds it the same user request and retrieved documents the agent saw. Per lesson 79, what is the problem?
options: An LLM classifier is too slow for a real-time approval path

The classifier reads the same untrusted content as the request being evaluated, so adversarial text can influence it into marking the request low-risk; risk classification should be deterministic policy logic as the authoritative signal, with LLM-assisted classification only as optional input that a deterministic layer re-checks
An LLM classifier cannot output a risk tier without fine-tuning
There is no problem as long as the classifier runs on a separate model from the agent
questions.explanation: The lesson follows AWS guidance that risk classification cannot rely on an LLM exposed to the same untrusted content as the request being evaluated, because adversarial content could influence the classifier into marking the request as low-risk. Deterministic logic (policy engines, rule-based classifiers) is the authoritative signal; LLM-assisted classification is an optional input a deterministic layer re-checks.

questions.question: An operations agent starts making anomalous writes at 2am. The on-call engineer wants to kill it. Which sequence does lesson 79 prescribe, and why that order?
options: Stop the container, then page the team, then look at logs later
Revoke the credentials first, then capture the snapshot, and skip notifying dependents to avoid panic

Capture a forensic snapshot of memory, active sessions, and pending operations, then revoke credentials (deny-all on the role while preserving it), then broadcast the quarantine event so dependent workflows trip their circuit breakers; evidence comes first because recovery destroys it, and authority is what actually stops the agent
Pause new intake and let in-flight tasks finish, which is sufficient containment for any anomaly
questions.explanation: The lesson gives the order as snapshot, revoke, notify. Evidence first because recovery destroys it, authority second because permissions are the real capability, notification third so downstream workflows can activate circuit breakers. It also names two anti-patterns: quarantine by stopping the process without revoking credentials (the agent restarts with the same reach), and relying on a human to trigger quarantine at all.

questions.question: A finance team reviews 150 agent-proposed payments a day. Six weeks in, the approval log shows most decisions complete in under five seconds, and one bad payment gets approved by a reviewer who says they 'assumed the queue was pre-checked.' Which fix matches lesson 79?
options: Add a second approval step for every payment, since more review means more safety
Remove the queue entirely and let the agent pay autonomously, since reviewers clearly are not adding value
Trust the reviewers, because a five second decision is normal for an experienced specialist

Treat the fast approvals as a fatigue signal: risk-tier the gate so only actions where judgment changes the outcome need review, put the action, reason, actor, effect, evidence and confidence on the approval card so a genuine refusal is possible, and log reviewer identity and timestamps so the gate can be audited
questions.explanation: The lesson treats the share of approvals completed in a few seconds as the cheapest rubber-stamp detector, and describes rubber-stamping as the predictable result of routing more through review than judgment requires. The fixes it prescribes are risk-tiered approval, enough context on the review screen for a reviewer to genuinely say no (the action, reason, actor, effect), and logged decisions with reviewer identity and timestamps. Adding a second step to everything deepens the fatigue rather than fixing it.

questions.question: A bank licenses a vendor's credit-scoring engine, wraps it in its own onboarding portal, brands it as its decisioning platform, and uses it to approve or decline loan applications. Under the EU AI Act, how should the bank classify its role, and why does it matter?
options: Deployer only, because the vendor developed the model and therefore carries every obligation

Provider of that component, because Article 25 makes an organisation that puts its own name or trademark on a high-risk system the provider, which pulls the full provider duty set (documentation, risk management, conformity work) onto the bank
Neither provider nor deployer, because credit scoring is a minimal-risk use and the Act does not apply
Both provider and deployer in equal measure, so the bank can choose whichever duty set is cheaper to satisfy
questions.explanation: The lesson draws the line at branding and control. A deployer uses a system under its own authority; a provider develops a system or has one developed and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. Article 25 extends provider duties to anyone who puts their name or trademark on a high-risk system built by someone else. Credit scoring for access to essential services is a named high-risk category, so the bank's rebranding converts it into a provider for that component, with documentation, risk management and conformity obligations it did not have as a plain deployer.

questions.question: A compliance lead plans to have EU high-risk obligations satisfied by 2 August 2026, based on the original text of the AI Act. What correction does lesson 80 give, and what reason does the Commission give for the change?
options: The date stands, but only for systems embedded in regulated products such as medical devices

The obligations now start on 2 December 2027 for stand-alone systems and 2 August 2028 for AI embedded in regulated products, after the Digital Omnibus entered into force on 27 July 2026; the Commission cites harmonised standards not being ready, which put the original date in jeopardy
High-risk obligations were withdrawn entirely and replaced by the voluntary NIST AI RMF
The obligations started early on 2 February 2025 alongside the prohibited practices, so the plan is already late
questions.explanation: The lesson flags this as the part most summaries get wrong. The Commission proposed the Digital Omnibus on AI in November 2025, the co-legislators agreed a text in May 2026, and it entered into force on 27 July 2026. High-risk duties moved to 2 December 2027 for stand-alone systems and 2 August 2028 for AI embedded in regulated products. The stated reason was preparation: the harmonised standards that give the rules legal certainty were not ready, and the Commission's FAQ says the delay put the original date in jeopardy. Prohibitions did start in February 2025, but those are a different tier.

questions.question: Meridian's Triage agent rejects a candidate in March. In June, the candidate asks for an explanation under Colorado's automated decision-making law. The team kept 24-hour trace retention and edits prompts directly in a console with no versioning. What does lesson 80 say the failure is, and what is the fix?
options: No failure, because Colorado's 30-day explanation duty only covers the developer of the tool, not the deployer using it
No failure, because an adverse-action explanation only needs the model's name and the score threshold, both of which are in the policy document

The failure is evidentiary: the 30-day plain-language explanation requires decision-time context (inputs, retrieved documents, model version, prompt version), and 24-hour retention plus unversioned prompts means the team cannot reconstruct what the system actually did in March; keep trace logs long enough to answer within the statutory window and version prompts like code
The failure is legal only, so the team should amend the policy document to state that explanations are available on request and move on
questions.explanation: The lesson names the adverse-action explanation as one of two gaps that show up in almost every version of this exercise. Colorado requires deployers to give a plain-language description of the tool's role within 30 days of an adverse decision. Most agents produce a score and rationale at decision time and then lose the retrieval context, so if trace retention is 24 hours the team cannot answer in week three, let alone month three. The fix is to set retention against the longest statutory window and to version prompts and model changes so the team can say what the system was on the day of the disputed decision.

questions.question: A board deck states: "95 percent of AI pilots fail, only 39 percent of companies see EBIT impact, so fewer than half of programs pay back." The lesson objects to this sentence on what grounds?
options: The 95 percent figure comes from vendors rather than independent research, so it should be discarded entirely
The three figures are stale, because AI spending rose 49.5 percent, which invalidates earlier survey data

The figures measure different things: 95 percent is the share of analyzed deployments with no measurable P&L impact, 39 percent is the share of survey respondents attributing any enterprise EBIT impact, and they do not share a denominator
The 39 percent figure already includes the 95 percent failure rate, so citing both double-counts the same organizations
questions.explanation: The lesson walks through each source and then names the temptation to stack them into one arc, calling that a well-formatted composite no source supports. It also notes the 77 percent board figure has no performance content at all.

questions.question: In the invoice exception worked example, the case stays net positive even when the auto-clear rate falls to 10 percent. What does the lesson say explains that?
options: The remaining human reviews are cheaper because the agent prepared the evidence packet, so the workflow saves time even when the agent's proposal is not used automatically
Inference costs are so low that they are immaterial at any acceptance rate, so the benefit side carries the case alone
The baseline of 22 minutes per exception was overstated, so a lower auto-clear rate still beats it
Sample review of auto-cleared cases drops to zero as the rate falls, which releases enough hours to offset the slower tail
questions.explanation: The lesson states the value comes less from autonomy than from packet preparation that shortens every remaining human decision, and that the agent does not have to be right to be useful, only fast at making the next human decision faster.

questions.question: A team presents the invoice case with the same model and the same 40 percent auto-clear rate, but they removed the validator gate so analysts review every agent proposal from scratch. What does the lesson predict?
options: Payback stretches to about 9 months, because inference cost roughly doubles without caching
The case improves, because analysts keep full control and spend less time on policy exceptions
Hours freed falls to zero and the system costs about $13,053 a month while saving nothing, which is the shape of most failed pilots
The NPV stays near $1 million, because the build cost is already sunk by the time the gate is removed
questions.explanation: The lesson describes this exact variant: without the gate the analyst redoes the full 22 minutes to check the draft, hours freed drops to zero, and the cost stack of roughly $13,053 a month buys no savings. It also adds the error line that can make even the best sensitivity case a loss.

questions.question: A program has spent 180,000 dollars on the agent build and the ERP integration, 3,000 dollars a month on run and eval upkeep, and has no budget line for process redesign or capability building. Per the lesson, what does this spend shape indicate?
options: The program is in good shape, because the payback math from the invoice queue case does not depend on training spend
The build line is underweighted, so the auto-clear rate will stay below the 40 percent design assumption
The program is buying a capability it has not decided how to absorb, because capability building was treated as an implementation detail while technology took the money and attention
The ratio is correct, since the one to three to five pattern applies only to programs with a budget above one million dollars
questions.explanation: The lesson states the 1:3:5 finding as a diagnostic rather than a budget rule: if technology is the largest of the three numbers, the program is buying a capability it has not decided how to absorb, and it applies that reading directly to the 180,000 dollar build with no line for redesign or capability building.

questions.question: The AP lead reports that all six analysts finished the two-hour training session and asks whether the team is ready for go-live. According to the lesson, what is still missing?
options: A completion dashboard with per-analyst timestamps, so the sponsor can see the training landed

A proficiency gate: twenty real cases including the ugly ones, decisions scored by a reviewer against a stated threshold, a written note on deliberate departures, and a dated retry path for anyone who fails
A follow-up class scheduled thirty days after go-live to refresh the material once people have used the tool
Nothing, because finishing the session closes the knowledge stage and the ability stage follows automatically with practice
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the gap sits between knowledge and ability, that training completion indicates information was received rather than that it can be applied under real conditions, and it lists the four parts of a working gate: real evidence set, scored dry run, stated threshold, retry path with a date.

questions.question: A team has run the weekly triage for eight weeks and produced meeting notes every time, with no eval cases, no policy changes and no tool fixes. Per the lesson, what is happening and what is the fix?
options: The agent is performing well enough that no changes are needed, so the meetings should continue as passive monitoring
The intake schema needs more free-text fields, so analysts can describe problems in richer detail
The loop is capturing without closing, and the fix is to promote at least one corrected answer into the offline eval set each week and require it to be named in the notes
Triage should move to a monthly cadence so each item has time to mature before a decision is made
questions.explanation: The lesson treats the output of a feedback loop as a change to the system, calls a loop with zero conversions for two weeks decorative, and prescribes exactly that fix: promote at least one corrected answer into the offline eval set and name it, since the corrected answer is the field that becomes a test case.
